name: Methoxypropylamino cyclohexenylidene ethoxyethylcyanoacetate

lead: This filter, abbreviated MCE, absorbs long-wave UVA1 (360 to 400 nm, peak 385 nm), the range tied to wrinkling and pigmentation. L'Oreal markets it as Mexoryl 400, and La Roche-Posay sells it as UVMune.
It was developed by L'Oreal and BASF. The EU approved it in 2019 at up to 3%, and Australia followed in 2025. No peer-reviewed clinical studies of the filter were found.

paras: It is used in La Roche-Posay and other L'Oreal-group sunscreens, as part of a daily facial SPF with other filters. Per Wikipedia it is used only in L'Oreal-group products.
Public toxicology information is limited to regulatory opinions and concentration limits. The US FDA does not currently recognise it for sunscreens.

angle.text: This L'Oreal filter (Mexoryl 400, UVMune) targets long-wave UVA1, the range tied to wrinkling and pigmentation, and is promoted in La Roche-Posay sunscreens. It gained EU approval in 2019; no published human trials show appearance outcomes.

lead: Methoxypropylamino cyclohexenylidene ethoxyethylcyanoacetate (MCE) is an organic UV filter for sunscreens that absorbs long-wave UVA1 radiation. L'Oreal markets it as Mexoryl 400 and its subsidiary La Roche-Posay sells it as UVMune.[1] People who use sunscreen to keep skin tone even and slow visible aging look to it because it covers the 370 to 400 nm band that conventional filters leave less protected, a band linked to pigmentation and skin aging.[2][3]

It has an absorption maximum at 385 nm, in the UVA1 range (360 to 400 nm).[1] The EU approved it as a cosmetic UV filter in 2019 at up to 3%, and Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration followed in 2025 at the same limit; the same page states that the US FDA does not currently recognise it.[1]

Several randomized, intra-individual studies have compared sunscreens with and without the filter on pigmentation and facial aging signs, and a 2025 case report describes severe allergic contact dermatitis to it.[2][3][4][5]

paras: The compound is a yellow solid with a molar mass of about 322 g/mol and dissolves in ethanol and several cosmetic solvents.[1] Its absorption peak at 385 nm lies at the long-wave end of UVA, a region that other filters cover less strongly.[1][2]

The EU approval in 2019 followed an opinion of the Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety, which set the 3% cap.[1][3] Australia approved it in 2025 at the same level.[1] According to Wikipedia, it is used only in L'Oreal products, and it has no FDA recognition for US use.[1]

Studies describe the premise as a photoprotection gap: UV up to about 370 nm is well blocked by current sunscreens while 370 to 400 nm wavelengths pass, and UVA1 is linked to pigmentation and aging.[2][3] Sunscreens containing the filter are sold with the UVMune name and discussed as broad-spectrum products.[1]

A 2025 case report in Contact Dermatitis describes severe allergic contact dermatitis caused by the filter.[4] In the Chinese single-centre study of a Mexoryl 400 sunscreen, no adverse reactions were reported.[6]

A 4-week outdoor randomized, intra-individual study in 52 Brazilian women applied an SPF50 sunscreen with 1% MCE to one half of the face and the same SPF50 without it to the other before one hour of daily sun exposure; expert graders found significant differences favouring the MCE side for crow's feet and upper-lip wrinkles, upper-lip pigmentation, texture and vascular abnormalities.[5]

An 8-week outdoor trial in 113 women in Brazil and China used 3% MCE on half the face and forearm, with skin colour change by chromametry as the primary endpoint and expert and naive panel grading of pigmentation, aging and radiance as other endpoints.[2] A study in the JID Innovations paper combined a 3D skin model with a 19-volunteer randomized trial and reported that adding MCE extended absorption to 400 nm and reduced UVA1-induced alterations and pigmentation.[3]

A single-centre study of 60 Chinese adults using a sunscreen containing Mexoryl 400 and other filters for 4 weeks reported reduced skin melanin (13.49%), redness (9.84%), forehead sebum (22.70%) and increased hydration (38.44%).[6] The sunscreen in that study had multiple components, so effects cannot be attributed to MCE alone.

timeline.event: Approved in the EU as a cosmetic UV filter up to 3%.[1]
JID Innovations paper reports in vitro and randomized trial results.[3]

Approved by Australia's TGA up to 3%; 4-week Brazilian trial and a contact dermatitis case report published.[1][4][5]
